\subsection{Transfer-learning protocol}
\label{sec:sota-protocol}

Two pretrained architectures were adapted to EuroSAT:
MobileNetV2~\cite{sandler2018mobilenetv2}, and EfficientNet-B0~\cite{tan2019efficientnet}.
Both start from ImageNet weights and the final linear layer of each classifier was replaced by a
new ten-class prediction layer. Every run uses the same stratified split as Models A and B,
random seed, augmentation, training-split normalisation statistics, batch
size of 128, 30-epoch budget and Colab Tesla~T4 as the machine to run on.
The checkpoint was chosen by lowest validation loss, before testing.

Once the new prediction layer is in place, there were two cases to choose from, either
keep the pretrained backbone \emph{frozen}, or \emph{fine-tune} it. Each
network was tested using both methods, to decide whether fine-tuning all parameters improves the result.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Frozen.} In this case, only the new prediction layer was trained, with Adam Optimizer at
  a learning rate of $10^{-3}$. The CNN backbone acts as a fixed feature extractor,
  and its batch-normalisation statistics were held at their original ImageNet values.
  \item \textbf{Fine-tuned.} In this case, every weight was trained, starting from the
  ImageNet weights, with Adam at a learning rate of $10^{-4}$. Here we chose a learning rate
  below the frozen-backbone rate to limit changes to the pretrained filters while
  the new classifier learns.
\end{itemize}

Our main runs keep the input at $64\times64$, which is the original resolution that the custom
models see. Because ImageNet networks are
designed for $224\times224$ input, the experiment was repeated for each network
with the $64\times64$ images upsampled to $224\times224$, for both the frozen and fine-tuned cases. Each $224\times224$
pair keeps the other training settings fixed and uses the same Tesla T4,
so the comparison measures the effect of changing the input resolution.

\subsection{Results}
\label{sec:sota-results}

  \caption{Pretrained lightweight models on the EuroSAT test split. Precision

Table~\ref{tab:sota-comparison} lists the results for both training strategies.
\emph{Parameters} and \emph{Size} are identical for the frozen and fine-tuned
runs of a network: freezing changes which parameters are updated, not the
inference architecture or saved-state size.  \emph{Trained} counts the
updated parameters.  In the frozen case, the prediction layer contains under
one per cent of the network's parameters.  The storage column does not measure
peak training memory.  The strategies also use different learning rates and
batch-normalisation update policies, as described above.

Fine-tuning improves accuracy, precision and recall for both networks.
This is consistent with a domain difference between ImageNet's object
photographs and EuroSAT's overhead satellite imagery.  A frozen model can
only re-weight its existing features, while fine-tuning adapts the backbone.
These experiments do not isolate the domain difference from the learning-rate
and batch-normalisation changes in the two training strategies.

The two architectures also rank differently under the two strategies described above. Frozen,
EfficientNet-B0 is clearly the weaker network, despite having almost twice
MobileNetV2's parameters. In the Fine-tuned case, the two networks are practically at the same level. The
gap between the frozen runs shows how well each network's ImageNet features happen to
transfer to $64\times64$ overhead satellite images.
Once fine-tuned, EfficientNet-B0 has only a small observed accuracy advantage
and nearly twice the saved-weight storage.  Without repeated seeds, this
small gap does not establish a reliable ranking.  MobileNetV2 is the more
storage-efficient pretrained option in these runs.

The supplementary rows show that upsampling to $224\times224$ gives both frozen backbones a gain of
several points, but the fine-tuned models gain less than one.  Upsampling
changes the scale at which the fixed filters see the image; it adds no new
sensor detail.  The smaller gain after fine-tuning suggests that adaptation
at native resolution reduces the need for upsampling in these runs.  For each
network, the fine-tuned $64\times64$ model outperforms the frozen
$224\times224$ one. It also does about $(224/64)^2\approx12$ times fewer
operations per image, because a convolution's cost scales with the $H\times W$
of its output. For an edge device,
fine-tuning at native resolution is the cheaper way to get accuracy.

Even the smallest of these models is one to two orders of magnitude larger on
disk than Model~B (Table~\ref{tab:custom-comparison}). Whether the extra accuracy is worth that memory is the
question Section~\ref{sec:task6} answers.

The training curves (Figures~\ref{fig:sota-loss}--\ref{fig:efficientnet-224-loss})
show the difference between the two strategies for both networks. Each frozen
run levels off at a higher loss than its fine-tuned counterpart. The frozen
EfficientNet-B0 curves are also visibly noisier than MobileNetV2's. After the
first few epochs both of its losses fluctuate instead of
settling, and at $224\times224$ the lowest validation loss happens to fall early,
so its selected checkpoint comes early in the run. The fine-tuned curves of
both networks reach lower losses than their frozen counterparts.

The aggregate histories do not establish the cause of the frozen
EfficientNet-B0 fluctuations.  Cross-entropy is sensitive to prediction
confidence, so loss can change while accuracy changes little.  Similar
accuracy across epochs does not show that the same images retain the same
predicted labels; the saved histories contain no per-image probabilities.

The backbones also use different activations.  EfficientNet-B0 uses the
unbounded SiLU (Swish) activation~\cite{tan2019efficientnet}, while MobileNetV2
uses ReLU6~\cite{sandler2018mobilenetv2}, discussed in
Section~\ref{sec:activation-choice}.  The committed runs do not measure pooled
feature magnitudes or isolate activation choice as a cause of the noisy loss.
The fluctuations make checkpoint selection sensitive to the validation-loss
minimum, which need not occur at the maximum-accuracy epoch.  Every reported
test result still uses the same lowest-validation-loss selection rule.

The confusion matrices of the fine-tuned $64\times64$ models
(Figures~\ref{fig:mobilenetv2-confusion} and~\ref{fig:efficientnet-confusion})
place the remaining errors in the same few class pairs for both networks.
Highway and River are confused in both directions, possibly because at $64\times64$ both are
thin features a few pixels wide. The agricultural and vegetation
classes (AnnualCrop, PermanentCrop, Pasture and HerbaceousVegetation), which
differ mainly in texture, account for a large share of the rest of the errors.
